BENEFICIARY RIGHTS AND STANDING UNDER A REVOCABLE TRUST — BEFORE AND AFTER THE SETTLOR'S DEATH (PROB. CODE §§ 15800-15802, 16069, 17200, 24; ESTATE OF GIRALDIN; BAREFOOT V. JENNINGS; DRAKE V. PINKHAM) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · January 1, 2026

WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This sheet surveys California law on a single question: who may enforce a revocable trust, and when. It collects the text of Probate Code sections 15800, 15801, 15802, 16069, 17200 and 24, and the two California Supreme Court decisions that construe them — Estate of Giraldin (2012) 55 Cal.4th 1058 and Barefoot v. Jennings (2020) 8 Cal.5th 822. It records what those authorities say about three periods: while the settlor is alive and competent, while the trust is still revocable but no competent person holds the power to revoke, and after the settlor's death. Two words recur. 'Revocable' describes a trust the holder of the power can still revoke, in whole or in part; the statutes speak of 'the person holding the power to revoke' rather than of the settlor, and the two are not always the same person. 'Beneficiary' is a defined term, and this sheet reproduces the definition rather than paraphrasing it. Prepared by Jane Doe on January 1, 2026, consulted with reference to The Doe Family Trust, settlor John Doe, trustee Mary Roe, and beneficiary Alex Doe. Recording those names is for the reader's own file: no clause in this sheet asserts anything about that trust or those persons, states whether anyone has or lacks standing in a particular matter, or recommends a course of action.

WHO HOLDS A BENEFICIARY'S RIGHTS WHILE THE TRUST IS REVOCABLE (PROB. CODE § 15800(A))
Probate Code section 15800, subdivision (a), sets a default that reverses the ordinary arrangement of trust law. Except to the extent that the trust instrument otherwise provides, or where the joint action of the settlor and all beneficiaries is required, the subdivision applies 'during the time that a trust is revocable and at least one person holding the power to revoke the trust, in whole or in part, is competent'. During that time, paragraph (1) provides that the person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the rights afforded beneficiaries under Division 9 of the code, and paragraph (2) provides that the duties of the trustee are owed to the person holding the power to revoke. The subdivision is written in terms of competence and revocability, not in terms of whether the settlor is alive: it ceases to apply either when the trust is no longer revocable or when no person holding the power to revoke remains competent.

CONSENT AND NOTICE WHILE THE TRUST IS REVOCABLE (PROB. CODE §§ 15801, 15802)
Two neighbouring sections carry the same allocation into particular acts. Section 15801, subdivision (a), provides that in any case where the consent of a beneficiary may be given or is required before an action may be taken, during the time that a trust is revocable and the person holding the power to revoke is competent, that person and not the beneficiary has the power to consent or withhold consent; subdivision (b) states that the section does not apply where the joint consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries is required by statute. Section 15802 provides that notwithstanding any other statute, during the same period, a notice that is to be given to a beneficiary shall be given to the person holding the power to revoke and not to the beneficiary. Unlike section 15800, neither section was rewritten in the 2021 and 2022 amendments described elsewhere in this sheet; both still read in the singular, 'the person holding the power to revoke the trust is competent'.

THE ACCOUNTING EXCEPTION FOR REVOCABLE TRUSTS (PROB. CODE § 16069)
Probate Code section 16069, subdivision (a), lists circumstances in which the trustee is not required to account to the beneficiary, provide the terms of the trust to a beneficiary, or provide requested information under section 16061. Paragraph (1) of that subdivision names the case of a beneficiary of a revocable trust, as provided in subdivision (a) of section 15800, for the period when the trust may be revoked; paragraph (2) names the case where the beneficiary and the trustee are the same person. Subdivision (b) then carves back from subdivision (a): notwithstanding subdivision (a), in the case of a revocable trust, if no person holding the power to revoke is competent, the trustee's duties to account are owed to the beneficiaries specified in section 15800, subdivision (b)(2). The statute is therefore drafted as a cross-reference: the scope of the exception in subdivision (a)(1) is fixed by what section 15800, subdivision (a), covers.

THE PETITION GATE AND THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF 'BENEFICIARY' (PROB. CODE §§ 17200, 24)
Probate Code section 17200, subdivision (a), opens the trust chapter's petition procedure with an express cross-reference to the revocable-trust rule: except as provided in section 15800, a trustee or beneficiary of a trust may petition the court concerning the internal affairs of the trust or to determine the existence of the trust. Subdivision (b) then lists proceedings that count as concerning internal affairs; paragraph (3) of that list is 'Determining the validity of a trust provision.' Who counts as a 'beneficiary' for this purpose is fixed by section 24, subdivision (c), which provides that as it relates to a trust the word means a person who has any present or future interest, vested or contingent. Read together, the two sections make the class of persons who may petition wider than the class of persons currently entitled to distributions, while section 15800 postpones when the members of that class may exercise the right.

ESTATE OF GIRALDIN ON WHOM THE TRUSTEE SERVES WHILE THE SETTLOR LIVES
In Estate of Giraldin (2012) 55 Cal.4th 1058, the California Supreme Court read section 15800 as settling the direction of the trustee's duty during the settlor's competent lifetime. Quoting the version of the section then in force, the court said the italicized language of what was then subdivision (b) makes clear that so long as the settlor is alive the trustee owes a duty solely to the settlor and not to the beneficiaries, and that taken together the surrounding provisions meant the beneficiaries there 'were powerless to act regarding the trust' during the settlor's competent lifetime. The court accepted the Court of Appeal's premise on this point, stating that the trustee owes no duty to the beneficiaries while the settlor is alive and competent and that this lack of a duty does not retroactively change after the settlor dies. What the court rejected was a different proposition, addressed in the next clause: that the absence of a lifetime duty to beneficiaries also disposes of their standing, after the settlor's death, to complain of a breach of the duty owed to the settlor.

ESTATE OF GIRALDIN — STANDING AFTER THE SETTLOR'S DEATH FOR A LIFETIME BREACH
The question the Supreme Court decided in Estate of Giraldin was whether, after the settlor dies, the beneficiaries of what had been a revocable trust have standing to sue the trustee for breach of the fiduciary duty owed to the settlor during the settlor's lifetime. The court held that they do, and framed the holding by reference to harm: after the settlor has died and can no longer protect his own interests, the beneficiaries have standing to claim a violation of the trustee's duty to the settlor to the extent that violation harmed the beneficiaries' interests. Restating the holding at the close of its discussion, the court described it as a holding about standing alone — that after the settlor's death the beneficiaries have standing to assert a breach of the fiduciary duty the trustee owed to the settlor to the extent that breach harmed the beneficiaries. The court also recorded a negative survey result: it was aware of no statute, judicial decision, or other authority, from California or any other state, denying such standing.

ESTATE OF GIRALDIN ON READING §§ 15800, 16069 AND 17200 TOGETHER
Two of the statutory readings that carried the result in Estate of Giraldin bear directly on the accounting and petition provisions reproduced earlier in this sheet. On section 16069, the court acknowledged that the statutory language is somewhat ambiguous and may indeed be read as the trustee argued, but concluded that the section must be read in context with the cross-referenced section 15800, and declined to read section 16069 to mean that the trustee never has to provide an accounting even after the trust becomes irrevocable. On section 17200, the court observed that nothing in section 15800 limits the ability of beneficiaries to petition the court after the trust becomes irrevocable, and, reading section 17200 with the definition in section 24, subdivision (c), that a contingent beneficiary may petition the court subject only to the limitations provided in section 15800.

WHAT ESTATE OF GIRALDIN EXPRESSLY DID NOT DECIDE
Estate of Giraldin is explicit about the limits of its own decision. Having held that standing exists, the court stated that it expressed no view regarding the merits of the particular case before it, and remanded so that the Court of Appeal could decide the other issues it had not reached. The court also declined to resolve a timeliness question that had been raised throughout the litigation: it recorded that the trustee had argued in both the trial court and the Court of Appeal that the action was time-barred by the statute of limitations or by the doctrine of laches, said that it expressed no opinion on that point, and held only that the action was not premature merely because the life beneficiary was still living. A grant of standing under this decision therefore leaves both the merits and the timeliness of any such claim open.

THE SECTION THE SUPREME COURT QUOTED IN 2012 IS NOT THE SECTION IN FORCE TODAY
A reader comparing Estate of Giraldin with the current code will find that the court's quotation of section 15800 no longer matches the statute. In 2012 the court set the section out as applying 'during the time that a trust is revocable and the person holding the power to revoke the trust is competent', with the two operative rules appearing as subdivisions (a) and (b) — which is why the opinion speaks of 'section 15800, subdivision (b)' when it means the rule that the trustee's duties are owed to the person holding the power to revoke. In the section as it now reads, the same two rules appear as paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (a); the trigger has been rewritten to reach the case where 'at least one person holding the power to revoke the trust, in whole or in part, is competent'; and a new subdivision (b) addresses the opposite case, where no such person is competent. The current subdivision (b) is therefore a different provision from the subdivision (b) the Supreme Court cited.

WHEN NO COMPETENT PERSON HOLDS THE POWER TO REVOKE (PROB. CODE § 15800(B), (C))
Subdivision (b) of section 15800 governs the period in which a trust is still revocable but no person holding the power to revoke it, in whole or in part, is competent. Subject to the same two exceptions as subdivision (a), the trustee must within 60 days of receiving information establishing the incompetency of the last person holding the power to revoke give notice of the subdivision's application and a true and complete copy of the trust instrument and any amendments to each beneficiary to whom the trustee would be required or authorized to distribute income or principal if the settlor had died as of the date of receipt of the information; if the trust has been completely restated, superseded instruments and amendments need not be included. Paragraph (2) shifts the duties to account at least annually and to provide information requested under section 16061 to that same class of beneficiaries, and paragraphs (3) and (4) address beneficiaries whose interests are conditional. Subdivision (c) provides that incompetency for these purposes may be established by the method specified in the trust instrument, as amended or restated, or by a judicial determination of incompetency.

BAREFOOT V. JENNINGS — STANDING OF A BENEFICIARY DISINHERITED BY AMENDMENT
Barefoot v. Jennings (2020) 8 Cal.5th 822 answered a question section 15800 does not reach, because the settlor there had already died. The Supreme Court framed the issue as whether a person disinherited by amendments made shortly before the settlor's death — one not named in the trust's final iteration — has standing to challenge those amendments in probate court on grounds such as incompetence, undue influence, or fraud. Disagreeing with the Court of Appeal, the court held that the Probate Code grants standing in probate court to individuals who claim that trust amendments eliminating their beneficiary status arose from incompetence, undue influence, or fraud, and stated the rule as one that turns on the allegations: when a plaintiff claims to be a rightful beneficiary of a trust if the challenged amendments are deemed invalid, she has standing to petition under section 17200. On the role of section 15800, the court's statement was brief — because the settlor had died, the section was no longer relevant. It collects the text of Probate Code sections 15800, 15801, 15802, 16069, 17200 and 24, and the two California Supreme Court decisions that construe them — Estate of Giraldin (2012) 55 Cal.4th 1058 and Barefoot v. Jennings (2020) 8 Cal.5th 822. It records what those authorities say about three periods: while the settlor is alive and competent, while the trust is still revocable but no competent person holds the power to revoke, and after the settlor's death. Two words recur. 'Revocable' describes a trust the holder of the power can still revoke, in whole or in part; the statutes speak of 'the person holding the power to revoke' rather than of the settlor, and the two are not always the same person. 'Beneficiary' is a defined term, and this sheet reproduces the definition rather than paraphrasing it. Recording those names is for the reader's own file: no clause in this sheet asserts anything about that trust or those persons, states whether anyone has or lacks standing in a particular matter, or recommends a course of action.

Probate Code section 15800, subdivision (a), sets a default that reverses the ordinary arrangement of trust law. Except to the extent that the trust instrument otherwise provides, or where the joint action of the settlor and all beneficiaries is required, the subdivision applies 'during the time that a trust is revocable and at least one person holding the power to revoke the trust, in whole or in part, is competent'. During that time, paragraph (1) provides that the person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the rights afforded beneficiaries under Division 9 of the code, and paragraph (2) provides that the duties of the trustee are owed to the person holding the power to revoke. The subdivision is written in terms of competence and revocability, not in terms of whether the settlor is alive: it ceases to apply either when the trust is no longer revocable or when no person holding the power to revoke remains competent.

expectedJSON.body: Barefoot v. Jennings (2020) 8 Cal.5th 822 answered a question section 15800 does not reach, because the settlor there had already died. The Supreme Court framed the issue as whether a person disinherited by amendments made shortly before the settlor's death — one not named in the trust's final iteration — has standing to challenge those amendments in probate court on grounds such as incompetence, undue influence, or fraud. Disagreeing with the Court of Appeal, the court held that the Probate Code grants standing in probate court to individuals who claim that trust amendments eliminating their beneficiary status arose from incompetence, undue influence, or fraud, and stated the rule as one that turns on the allegations: when a plaintiff claims to be a rightful beneficiary of a trust if the challenged amendments are deemed invalid, she has standing to petition under section 17200. On the role of section 15800, the court's statement was brief — because the settlor had died, the section was no longer relevant. The court also set out the sequence a court follows on a standing challenge, which is to determine standing first by treating the properly pled allegations as true.
